bean-salad-yellow-and-or-green-string-be.title: Bean Salad, Yellow and/or Green String Beans

content.title: About
content.content: Bean salad made from yellow and/or green string beans is prepared with fresh pods, often combined with onion, carrot, vinegar, oil and spices. The beans retain a crisp texture after a short blanch, and their bright colour makes the dish visually appealing.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: String beans belong to the legume family and are cultivated worldwide.
Yellow beans are a cultivar lacking chlorophyll but retaining most nutrients.
Beans are rich in antioxidants, especially carotenoids that give the yellow colour.
Traditionally the salad is served in summer when beans are at peak freshness.
In some cuisines (e.g., Indian) beans are used as a spiced stir‑fry called “pakora”.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber supports healthy digestion, promotes satiety and helps regulate blood glucose levels.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity and participates in collagen synthesis, supporting skin and blood‑vessel health.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and is especially important for pregnant women.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Bean salad contains virtually no saturated fat, making it suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: It provides potassium, magnesium and iron, which support heart and muscle function.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans, ranging from skin rashes to severe symptoms.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; a brief blanching step helps lower its level.

items.title: Raw bean toxins
items.content: Raw beans contain lectins that can cause food poisoning; proper cooking neutralises them.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Blanch the beans for 3–5 minutes until crisp‑tender, then shock in ice water. Toss with olive oil, vinegar, mustard, finely chopped onion, grated carrot and fresh herbs. Optional additions include toasted nuts or seeds for extra crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3–4 days. Fresh pods keep best in a plastic bag in the vegetable drawer, where they stay crisp for up to 5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Dates are sweet fruits of the date palm (Phoenix dactylifera), native to the Middle East and North Africa. They have soft, sticky flesh with a caramel-like flavor and one elongated pit. Dates are eaten fresh and dried, added to desserts, baked goods, porridge, and smoothies, and used as a natural sweetener.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Date palms have been cultivated for thousands of years and bear fruit for a long time.
During Ramadan, Muslims traditionally break their fast with dates.
The best-known varieties are Medjool and Deglet Noor.
Dried dates are very sweet because they contain a lot of natural sugars.
Dates are made into paste and syrup, which are used in place of sugar.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and helps you feel full for longer.

items.title: Contain potassium
items.content: Potassium supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Contain magnesium
items.content: Magnesium plays a role in muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Contain antioxidants
items.content: The polyphenols and carotenoids in dates have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Quick source of energy
items.content: Thanks to natural sugars, dates provide energy quickly, which makes them handy as a snack.

items.title: Sugar and calories
items.content: Dates are very sweet and high in calories, so portions should be moderate, and people with diabetes need to count them in their diet.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: The fructose and sorbitol in dates can cause bloating and discomfort in some people.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: People with kidney disease who need to limit potassium should consult a doctor.

items.title: Pits and additives
items.content: The pit can damage teeth, and some dried dates contain sulfites or syrup.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dates can be eaten as a snack, stuffed with nuts, cream cheese, or peanut butter, or added to smoothies, porridge, yogurt, and baked goods. They are made into a paste to replace sugar in desserts. Remove the pits before using.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried dates in an airtight container in a cool, dry place; they keep longer in the refrigerator and even longer in the freezer. Keep fresh dates in the refrigerator. Discard dates that are moldy, smell sour, or show signs of fermentation.

content.title: About
content.content: Gelatin Dessert, Sugar Free (5066) is a ready‑to‑eat gelatin‑based dessert sweetened with low‑calorie sweeteners instead of sugar. It retains the classic soft texture of jelly, offers a light fruit flavor, and is suitable for people monitoring blood‑sugar levels.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Gelatin desserts became popular in Europe during the 19th century.
Sugar‑free versions often use stevia or erythritol, which do not raise the glycemic index.
The product can fit into low‑carb and keto diets.
Gelatin is derived from collagen, typically sourced from pork or beef bones and skin.
Sugar‑free jellies are frequently fortified with vitamin C and B‑complex for enhanced taste.

items.title: Low Calorie Content
items.content: The absence of sugar makes the dessert suitable for weight control and reduces overall caloric intake.

items.title: Joint Support
items.content: Gelatin is rich in collagen, which may help strengthen cartilage and tendons.

items.title: No Glycemic Spike
items.content: Low‑glycemic sweeteners do not cause rapid blood‑glucose spikes.

items.title: Rich in B‑Vitamins
items.content: Some variants are enriched with vitamins B6 and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Easy Digestion
items.content: The jelly dissolves quickly in the stomach, providing a fast source of energy without heaviness.

items.title: Gelatin Allergy
items.content: A minority of individuals may experience allergic reactions to gelatin, manifesting as skin rashes or gastrointestinal symptoms.

items.title: Sweetener Sensitivity
items.content: Large amounts of erythritol can cause mild gas or diarrhea in sensitive people.

items.title: Not Vegetarian/Vegan
items.content: Gelatin is animal‑derived, so the product is unsuitable for vegetarian or vegan diets.

items.title: Additive Content
items.content: Some versions may contain artificial flavors and preservatives that not everyone prefers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sugar‑free gelatin dessert chilled in individual cups. It can be garnished with fresh berries, mint leaves, or a sprinkle of nuts for added texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 2‑4 °C in a sealed container. Once opened, it is best consumed within 7‑10 days. Discard if the taste, smell, or texture changes.
